In these cases, the diagnosis of CNO can be made, combining clinical findings (localized bone pain, swelling, and warmth in the affected areas) and laboratory tests (including testing for mycobacteria) with radiographic techniques. panels.rationale: Whole-body bone scintigraphy (panel A, stored as the complete single image) from a case of nonbacterial osteitis of the clavicle, i.e. the CRMO spectrum, showing a single intense radiotracer 'hot spot' in the right clavicle, a classic CRMO site. Real patient image; no third-party restriction indicated. Disease attribution rests on the disease-focused article title ('Nonbacterial osteitis of the clavicle') plus the specific captioned manifestation (clavicular hot spot), not on the broad topic alone. The hot spot represents a musculoskeletal inflammatory lesion (osteitis) on whole-body skeletal imaging, so it is mapped to the whole-body musculoskeletal-inflammation finding key; the exact scintigraphic manifestation is recorded in proposed_findings because no dedicated scintigraphy key exists. The presentation was monofocal ('a multifocal disease was unlikely'), a recognized less-common form of the CRMO/NBO spectrum, hence typicality 'variant'; the vocabulary defines no subtype, so subtype is null. Bone scintigraphy has no dedicated modality enum value, so modality is 'other'. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text, so both are unknown/null; no skin is shown, so skin_tone is null. Confidence reflects solid disease attribution tempered by the modality/multiplicity mismatch of the mapped finding.

in_text_mentions: Schematically, as explained previously, CRMO mainly consists of osseous lesions, whereas JSpA first includes joint anomalies, leading secondarily to osseous changes. In both diseases, MRI allows the visualization of most of the osteoarticular changes, including (1) bone marrow lesions, especially when using coronal T1-weighted and STIR sequences in addition to axial STIR images (Figure 4 and Figure 5), and (2) inflammatory lesions of the axial joints, which are best visualized on T1 sequences and include erosion, sclerosis, fat metaplasia, backfill and ankyloses [31].
CRMO, SAPHO and JSpA can show similarities in radiological findings (Figure 4 and Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Coronal STIR MRI of both lower extremities in a single acquisition, visually showing symmetric bright (edema) signal in the distal femoral metaphyses bilaterally. The caption explicitly describes multifocal distal femoral abnormalities with regional bone marrow edema, cortical thickening, and periostitis, and the in-text mention ties these MRI findings directly to the case's skeletal disease (CRMO). The disease-focused article title (CRMO and PSC in a child with ulcerative colitis) plus the specific captioned musculoskeletal manifestation support attribution to CRMO rather than PSC. Bilateral distal femoral metaphyseal marrow edema is a classic CRMO radiologic presentation. No panel labels, arrows, or scale bars are visible. Age, ethnicity, and skin tone are not assessable or stated for this panel.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial chest CT from a CRMO case report demonstrating sclerosis of the sternum and manubrium with sternoclavicular erosions; the in-text CT description confirms medial clavicular expansion/sclerosis with small lytic areas, a classic anterior chest-wall CRMO pattern. B: PET-CT fusion image from the same CRMO patient showing diffuse abnormal hypermetabolic uptake throughout the manubrium sternum with expansion of the manubrium and intense activity at the manubrial-sternal junction, corresponding to the sclerotic anterior chest-wall lesions seen on CT. C: Whole-body PET from the same CRMO patient demonstrating multifocal abnormal hypermetabolism matching sclerotic and partially lytic lesions in the sternum and bilateral clavicular heads, a classic multifocal CRMO distribution; physiologic uptake in brain, heart, salivary glands and urinary tract as stated in the caption.
